Title: Have WW been too safe in their card design?

Messages.Author: Chris Arthur
Messages.Body:
Here in Australia a local distributor has marked down Anarchs booster
boxes but no one in my playgroup wants to buy them. Why not? What's
going on? The reason most had was "What's Anarchs worth buying for?".
A whole box for Aranthebes?

I think WW have been too careful in the design of their library cards.
While it is an admirable goal to avoid printing overpowered cards like
RtI it seems to have had the unintended side effect of making most of
the cards fairly useless. The Anarchs set has cemented that idea for
me.

I did a quick and admittedly inconclusive scan of the EC 2003 decks to
see how many WW created cards were in the five decks. I found that
there were only 12 out of 425 library cards created by WW:

Jake Washington (FN) 1
Week of Nightmares (FN) 1
Khobar Towers (FN) 2
Treasured Samadji (FN) 1
PB: Montreal (SW) 2
Aranthebes (AN) 1
Art's Traumatic Essence (B) 2
Reins of Power (AN) 1
Year of Fortune (AN) 1

Off the top of my head I can think of a few more that are useful (e.g.
Enticement, Sanguine Instruction, PB: Madrid etc.) however after five
sets I would have expected there to be more good cards.

The new mechanics leave a little to be desired as well. Infernalism
has too high a cost and why does the first Anarch action cost two
blood???? Did they really think it would be that powerful?

I'd like to see the DT take more risks. So what if an overpowered card
comes along every now and then? We can always just ban it. :)

Chris.

At this point Anarchs is behind us. From what has been shown so far

shape. I'm looking forward to what they have for us in the future.

I agree with Chris on all accounts. But I also understand WW being
careful - the game balance of VtES is very delicate and fragile. As I
see it the old cards (the original set) is and should always be, the
"core set" and those cards should be the most played. And being forced
to ban new cards is no fun.

But in the case of the Anarch expansion (and ALL starter decks except
maybe the CE Ventrue one) I have to question WW愀 intentions... Do
they want to sell cards? Although I admire if they do not go
"Deciphery" with foils and infinte numbers of alternate versions of
popular cards just to sell more, they should try to make rares at
least playable (The example from EC 2003 speaks its own language, but
I think Bloodlines was realy nice rare-wise). And add sought-after
reprints in starters to get them off the store shelves. I look forward
to seeing the Black Hand expansion (I pray not getting to many of
those pesky Crusade-rares in the boosters I open).

So, WW could take good care of the game balance, but try to increase
sales a bit and in the same time make me smile when I open a booster!
What about that?

No, but *the cards* usable by anarchs are. Your playgroup just didn't
realize it yet.
Diversion provides, in just one card, an additional strike for free at
inferior (you won't find any other celerity card that does this) and
two damage prevention for free at inferior (same case with Fortitude).
Improvised Tactics provide a "fixed ranged signpost" of 2R *every
round*. OK, you'll have to use Trap to be effective, but it is still a
little above the usual.
Too many people are used to Blur and Immortal Grapple and Skin fo
Steel for many years, and these advantages in crypt selection, since
you don't need superior anymore, and in blood saving, didn't get
noticed yet. But they will.
Another problem is the way you should work anarch decks to be
valuable. Most people didn't realise that most of the time you should
think the crypt and the deck to be wholly anarch - unless you want to
risk cornercase situations. That means: throw in lots of Galaric's
Legacy and Go Anarch. The first is trifle, it will in fact help you
with masters hand jamming. Go Anarch will save your blood and won't
take you a precious action, since you untap immediately. Most people
didn't realize this.
I have an anarch version of Fatima Multi-Rush that works very well,
and will be better when I get some more Diversions. With this card
instead of Pursuit, I can mantain combat at zero blood cost, make a
new crypt with obf/cel weenies that will be able to use additionals,
and add lots of free damage prevention to an archetype deck that
didn't had much room for it (there's always some Drawing Out the Beast
around). The combat module could consist of Disguised Weapon,
Diversion, Taste of Vitae and Psyche!, and nothing more.

> comes along every now and then? We can always just ban it. :)

much: you have to put your brain working hard to build around some
cards. It's a challenge.
And even V:TES has its overpowered cards. They're discussed in this

Chris wrote:
> Here in Australia a local distributor has marked down Anarchs booster
> boxes but no one in my playgroup wants to buy them. Why not? What's

> going on? The reason most had was "What's Anarchs worth buying for?".

While an understandable viewpoint, you need to keep in mind that the
last two independant expansions, Bloodlines and Anarchs, were both
very narrow expansions. Thios doesn't mean that they weren't good and
well designed, but both of them had sort of a limited field of use.
Bloodlines had tons of new and exciting stuff, but unless you are
building a fringe strategy bloodline deck, you aren't going to use
most of the set. Anarchs as well--unless you are building an Anarch
specific strategy, most of the set isn't that useful--maybe 5-10% of
the cards in the set are general use while the rest require an Anarch
strategy.

This being said, I think both sets were very well designed and did
quite well what they wanted to do. But overall, both sets were more
"fun" sets than "competetive" sets (although there are certainly some
very good, winning strategies using Bloodlines clans--there are
probably similar winning strategies in the Anarchs set, but we haven't
really found them yet). But in any set, there are going to be good
general use vampires, and good general use cards. Off the top of my
head in Anarchs, in terms of good general use cards we got:

-Life in the City, which is very solid in the right deck.
-Cooler, which can be very handy (see the most recent Nosferatu
Newsletter :-)
-Bleeding the Vine, which is fringe but powerful.
-The various hold cards certainly have potential.
-Aranthebes, which is very potent.
-Blow Torch, which is a good, cheap weapon.
-Lots of very good vampires.
-Tons of easy to get reprinted protean cards (I finally have all the
Flesh of Marbles I need).

Even without making an Anarchs strategy (which I am yet to actually
do), I have found a great deal of potential in the Anarchs set.

> I think WW have been too careful in the design of their library cards.
> While it is an admirable goal to avoid printing overpowered cards like
> RtI it seems to have had the unintended side effect of making most of
> the cards fairly useless. The Anarchs set has cemented that idea for
> me.

How are most of the cards useless? Yeah, if you aren't making an
Anarch deck, a lot of the set isn't going to be playable. But if you
are making an Anarch deck, you have a lot of solid material to work
with. And if you aren't, there is a good supply of other good stuff
too.

> Off the top of my head I can think of a few more that are useful (e.g.
> Enticement, Sanguine Instruction, PB: Madrid etc.) however after five
> sets I would have expected there to be more good cards.

There are plenty of good new cards. All the new vampires are in heavy
use. Many Bloodlines strategies are very competetive. Anarch decks are
still being experimented with, and it seems likely that at some point
someone will come up with a scary one.

> I'd like to see the DT take more risks. So what if an overpowered card
> comes along every now and then? We can always just ban it. :)

There are plenty of potent cards in the new sets. But again, limited
in scope. I suspect that Black Hand will be much more general use.

-Peter

hope hope for BH card) that a card existed to allow you to make MORE
vampires infernal - a clear sign that the price is not too high.

where the vamps are infernal and Contagious to boot. Or notice how

2-player game' or 'not usable in a 2-player game' - certain portions
of the market would be really pissed that they're buying cards they'll
never (or almost never) even be *able* to play with. (And yes, there
are people out there who play V:tes as an almost-exclusively 2-person
game. Just not on this mailing list usually.)

I can't even say what is more conservative since I never played on
either continent. I'm south american :-)
The point here is, you can't use the number of new sets cards in
finals of a given tournament as a guide. I *could* say Final Nights
and Anarchs are overpowered since one of the last finals here
(Storyline Guarulhos, Brazil) had two Setites and one Giovanni, all of
them using some Anarch cards like the mentioned Unlicensed Taxicab.
But I'd just be trying to defend a point of view I already had, not
really analysing the state of the game now.
To me, it is *true* that the older strategies are still very efficient
- and that's good for the game -, but that's far different to say the
newest sets are too underpowered when some cards clearly give your
minions abilities they didn't have (additional strike for free at
inferior and such. anyone who did look carefully at anarch cards know
what these are).
And sincerely, waiting for a set and its cards to appear in the finals
of a tournament is negating your own skills on deckbuilding.
Anarchs has a lot of problems, but it brings on too many new
possibilities to anyone to say that has fully explored it in a few
months. It requires a new take on old assumptions, like the number of
masters on a combat deck. Would 20 masters be too much, when 5 of them
are trifles? Does it make hand jamming with masters less probable or
it would be the same as using 15 'regular' masters?
So what I can say as my opinion is: it doesn't matter what metagame is
"conservative" or not. Discarding a new set without even trying to
explore its possibilities is conservative though, specially when this
attitude is based on how many cards of that set had effectively won
something.

There are definitely some stinker cards in the new sets. Of course,

There are lots of ways to at least temporarily get inferior Daimonion.
Off the top of my head: Be a !Tremere (or impersonate to one) with an
Infernal Pact. Be any minion with tha (or with the Thaum item) and an
Infernal Familiar. Be absolutely any vampire with a Vial of Elder
Vitae (an uncommon in the Cam set, even, not at all hard to acquire.)
Be a Lasombra (or impersonating one) with a Cam Vitae Slave.
Impersonate one way or another to have a Baali teach you via Sanguine
Instruction. Play Ian Forestal.

> I agree my statement about banning cards was rash but notice you make
> the point about coaster cards - that's my point too. what else are
> bounty, blackmail, lobotomy etc. if not coasters?

Cards that still have use, either in a cornercase situation or in
sealed-deck formats. (One of the things I enjoy most about sealed-deck
games is the opportunity to put oddball cards to use without putting
you at a big disadvantage, admittedly.)

I don't think Lobotomy is any more a coaster than say Ravnos
Acceptance, Goodnight Sweet Prince or Werewolf Pack. While you may
find some cards in recent sets less than ideal, the percentage (as
noted elsewhere in this thread) of truly wretched cards in an
expansion is still better than it was in the past, in a lot of
people's opinions.

> Chris.

Well, I still think they are pretty stealth-bleedy, but in the
interest of getting a rabid poodle off my heels, I dialed it back
some. Minion control is..... I don't know what else to call it.
Being able to control your opponenet's access to minions. Other
examples would be SenseDep, Banishment, Temptation, etc.

A really good combat deck has the potential to just completely deny
your opponent(s) access to minions. Most strategies collapse under
those conditions. When faced with nothing but collapsed strategies,

bleed, or much pool gain.

I think we all agree that judging the power of a to-be-released card is
quite complicated even with a lot of playtesting. There are hundreds to
thousands of other cards that might interact with the new card in some way
so that it will be broken.

I further think it is near impossible to create perfectly balanced new cards
and so you have two options : aim high or aim low.

WotC has aimed very high some times in "that other game" and then aimed very
low for some expansions. This has created a lot of frustration for some
people, either because the expansion was all crap (anyone remember Homelands
or Fallen Empires ?) or so good that it killed all that was before (except
for alpha/beta).

WW on the other hand has tried to aim constantly a little bit low. This
resulted in some good yet balanced and some not-so-good ones (cards). Yet
all expansions WW has produced (and also WotC while still owning V:TES) are
worth buying to some amount, some more some less (Anarchs certainly being
the one where you don´t need THAT many boxes and Sabbat or Bloodlines
probably the most interesting one).

Which option do you prefer ?

BTW : I find it a challenging and interesting task to put some use to cards
that are widely considered as "crap".

tournament scene any time soon? Probably not, but that is ok.

are built to use them can really use them.

Some things we do know:

- The sizes of the North American and European player bases are
roughly equivalent.

- Americans tend to travel more frequently for V:TES events than
Europeans. Reasons for this include more gaming conventions in
the US, and fewer restrictions for travel (cost of gasoline and
language immediately pop into mind). This, however, is becoming
less and less the case, with the popularity of the game on the
rise in Europe, and a lessening of travel restrictions due to
the EU. More travel means more exposure to decks, strategies,
and playstyles and more homogenization of the metagame. Less
travel means that regional differences in decks, strategies, and
playstyles are pronounced. As such, the overall American metagame
is less heterogenous than the European metagame (though still
heterogenous).

- Americans have greater access to cards than Europeans. Reasons
for this include online discount ordering (more cards for your
money), better distribution, and more retailers who actually
carry the game. Greater access to cards results in greater ability
to explore new deck designs and strategies.

Things I think we know, but I could very well be wrong (and please
correct me if I am!):

- Americans have greater access to gaming space at gaming shops
than Europeans. This probably varies a lot from region to region
on both continents. However, it seems to be the case that more
shops in America have space for gaming than in Europe.

- European tournaments are larger, on average, than American
tournaments and occur less frequently, on average and per region,
than American tournaments. Robyn Tatu would probably be best
able to answer this. I think the above statement about the lower
access to gaming space in Europe has a lot to do with this.
Because Americans have greater access to gaming space at gaming
shops, they have greater access to tournament venues than Europeans,
resulting in more frequent tournaments. The larger number of
gaming conventions in the US also adds to the greater access to
tournament venues. Because there are fewer tournaments in
Europe, European players put more emphasis on attending the
tournaments that do happen, resulting in larger events (from what
I understand, Spain is a great example of this).

So, what is the result of all of this? Because of the lower amount
of travel and the lower access to cards, you'll find that there's
less diversity in European deck styles (and a greater reliance on
the tried and true) than in America. This has nothing to do with
the ability level or demeanor of the players in their respective
continents, and in my personal experience, I've found that the better
players in Europe and the better players in the US are equivalent in
playing ability, in deck design ability, and in ruthlessness.

Because of the larger tournament sizes in Europe, you see a difference
in the styles of decks you see in tournaments. Generally speaking,
the more players in a tournament, the more game wins and victory points
you need to make the finals. In particularly large tournaments, where
you might need 8 VP to make the finals, a greater emphasis is placed on
decks that have a higher capacity to get a lot of victory points at a
table. There are other deck styles that might win games more often, but
the sheer volume of players means that statistically more players will
have opportunities to sweep tables and otherwise accumulate lots of VP.
It becomes less about whether or not you win, and more about how you
win if you do win. As a result, you see more decks that have a lesser
chance of winning the game, but that can get more VP if they _do_ win,
knowing what is likely required to make the finals at all. One of the
deck styles that meets this description is Steath-Bleed.

> i am preety sure that a bsaic malk S&B would have the same succes in the
> states as it has in europe, people just don´t play them!

Given the same access to cards, the same restrictions on travel, the
same access to gaming space, and the same sizes of tournaments, you'd
get the same results in America and Europe. However, all of these
factors are different, so the results will be different. There's nothing
intrinsic about being an American or a European that would change things.

- Ben Peal, Prince of Boston

chance to influence a third minion;
- it helped me to cycle stealth cards. When I got out of Blackmail and
my prey decided it would be silly to keep trying to block, I got a
pretty annoying stealth hand jam.

Wolflord wrote:
> *I (and th eplayers I know)have (and for those of you who don't know

> where Belgium is, I'm European) never had any problems getting my
> cards in abundant quantities. Over the recent years I don't buy mine
> in Belgium anymore though, due to the fact that WW's distributors in
> Belgium have grown very scarse indeed, resulting in incredibly high
> prices.

By contrast, players from Bratislava, Slovakia often travel to Vienna
because their local game shop is _horrible_ about carrying V:TES cards.
While in Hungary, I had difficulty trading cards because the players
there wanted to _buy_ my cards instead. Why? They didn't have cards
to trade me! (it wasn't that they didn't have cards I wanted - they
didn't have much of a stock of cards at all)

On top of that, Americans have much greater access to discounted
boxes of cards (US$65/box through Potomac Distribution). For the
same money, we get a lot more cards.

> *I have to admit though, that I was under the impression (from reading
> this very newsgroup and watching the card prices in US) that US people
> had quite a lot of trouble getting their cards. I've never heard
> anybody in Europe saying things lik: "I need to get my hands on more
> Improvised tactics", or "Jeez, that Ian Forrestal is hard to find", so
> you've kinda surprised me.

Well, again, when we can get booster boxes for $65/box, card
availability is much less of an issue here.

> *Regarding to the amount of tournaments: I think that's a point of
> view. I can tell you that if I would find the time, I could go and
> play a tournament alkmost every week or 2 weeks, at the very least
> once a month. But it kinda peaks in certain months around here. In
> some periods I've known some of us to play 5 or 6 relatively big
> tournaments in under 3 weeks..

Again, it was a general statement, and certainly you'll find areas
in Europe where you can play frequently. You can also find areas
of the US where one plays less frequently. But hey, perhaps I'm
wrong. Heh...if I'm this bored, I should go look at the Event
Calendar. :)

Better yet, I could get the Create-A-Clan and EC2003 pictures sites
up and running. Those should be ready on Monday or Tuesday.
